title: Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf
hook: he arrived in Medina with nothing, asked for the market, grew rich, and kept giving

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abdullah ibn Umar, who stopped to pray where the Prophet had prayed. Your line was: in his footsteps. Which small sunnah did you copy, and did it stay with you? Day eight hundred forty.

Here is an offer almost too generous to hear. A man has just arrived in Medina from Mecca with nothing. His new brother, a man of the city named Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', says to him: I have more wealth than anyone among the helpers. Take half of it. And I have two wives; see which you like, and I'll divorce her so you can marry. That is in Sahih al-Bukhari. Half of everything, offered to a man who has just arrived. What would anyone say? The newcomer said no. Gently. Today: the man who turned down half a fortune and asked for directions instead.
screen: `A NEWCOMER WITH NOTHING.` → `TAKE HALF OF EVERYTHING.` → `HE SAID NO.`

segments.voice: His name was Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, one of the emigrants. When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, came to Medina, he paired emigrants with helpers as brothers, and Abd al-Rahman was paired with Sa'd. Listen to his answer to the offer of half. In Bukhari's report he says: may God bless you in your family and your wealth. Where is your market? And off he went. He traded, the report says, in cheese and butter, and he came back with a profit. Not long after, he turned up with traces of perfume on him, and he told the Prophet he had married. So the first thing to notice is a kind of dignity. He received a huge kindness, blessed the giver, and kept his hands open for work. Then the story goes on. The biographies remember him as becoming very wealthy, and as giving, again and again, in large amounts for the community and its poor. Tradition tells of whole caravans of goods given away; those accounts come from the sira, not from Bukhari, so hold them as stories the tradition tells. And remember where we met him earlier on this road: a rich man, fasting, unable to eat his meal for remembering Mus'ab and his short cloak. He was afraid, he said, that his reward had come early. That is the second thing to notice. Wealth did not make him easy. It made him careful. Rich and giving, and still afraid his reward had come too soon.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS, ONE OFFER.` · `WHERE IS YOUR MARKET?` · `CHEESE, BUTTER, AND A PROFIT.` · `RICH, AND STILL AFRAID.` · then, large: `RICH AND GIVING.`

segments.voice: The practice: give from a success. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that went well lately. A paycheck, a sale, a good grade, a job finished, a lucky break. Let yourself enjoy it for a breath. Then ask: what part of this could go to someone else? A bit of money to someone in need. Time, if money is tight. Credit, to the person who helped you get there. Breathe out, and choose one. If you pray, you can thank God for the success and ask that the giving be accepted. The bell holds the time.

Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. The emigrant who blessed his brother's offer, asked for the market, grew rich and kept giving. And this week's road: Zayd ibn Thabit, Mu'adh, Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, Anas, Ibn Umar, and today, Abd al-Rahman. Today's word.
Your line: rich and giving. Today, take one thing that went right for you, and pass a piece of it on before the day ends. Day eight hundred forty, and a week of companions done.

howItsDone: Muslims remember Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf's reply, 'where is your market?', as a picture of earning with dignity; giving from what one earns, through zakat and voluntary charity, is part of Muslim practice.

original.note: Arabic: servant of the Most Merciful, al-Rahman being one of God's names.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rich man who gave some money away.
what it means: a man who arrived with nothing, turned down half a fortune, worked his way up, and gave from what he earned.
what a scholar hears: the brotherhood of emigrants and helpers in Bukhari, and his own fear, at a full table, that his reward had come early.

Sa'd's 'I have more wealth than anyone among the helpers' is a paraphrase of his words in Bukhari 2048/3780; confirm wording.
